Senses.Explanation: Literally, to put out the tongue. The Chan record repeatedly makes this visible gesture part of public encounters, but does not give it one invariant emotional gloss. Huangbo involuntarily sticks out his tongue (不覺吐舌, “without realizing it, stuck out his tongue”) on hearing that Baizhang was deaf for three days after Mazu's shout. Elsewhere a visitor sticks out his tongue and says, “truly a dragon-elephant”; a monk leaves with his tongue out after a rebuke; and a later monk says that the teacher's gesture shows he has been caught out. Masters also deliberately use the action as an answer: Nanyuan sticks out his tongue when asked for “one word,” and Zhongqing opens his mouth and sticks out his tongue when asked what his appearance as abbot is for. Thus the ordinary bodily gesture is bent into an answer or demonstrative act in the teaching hall as well as remaining a recorded reaction; the texts themselves decide its local force, and this entry does not assign one motive to every occurrence.
Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 548 matches in 194 texts. The retained evidence covers involuntary reaction, spoken appraisal, answer to a one-word question, answer concerning an abbot's public function, and an adversarial interview. Formula searches yielded no corpus-wide verbal definition. Family revalidation against “tongue; capacity to speak” (舌頭) and the “broad, long tongue-mark” (廣長舌相) supports one action sense: reaction and deliberate answer are different deployments of the same bodily act, not different things under depth-gate item 8.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老僧昔被馬大師一喝。直得三日耳聾。黃檗聞舉。不覺吐舌。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baizhang says, ‘This old monk was once shouted at by Master Ma and was deaf for three days.’ Hearing it, Huangbo ‘without realizing it, stuck out his tongue.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。一言作麼生。師乃吐舌云。待我有廣長舌相。即向汝道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked, ‘What is one word like?’ Nanyuan sticks out his tongue and says, ‘Wait until I have the broad, long tongue-mark; then I will tell you.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 年復喝。師以手劃一劃。年吐舌曰。真是龍象。師曰。是何言歟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After another shout and the teacher's hand gesture, the visitor sticks out his tongue and says, ‘Truly a dragon-elephant’; the teacher challenges that statement.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：古佛出世，為一大事因緣。和尚出世，所為何事？師張口吐舌示之，曰：祇者箇，別更有？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked what his appearance as abbot is for, Zhongqing opens his mouth and sticks out his tongue to show it; the monk asks, ‘Only this—anything else?’

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “chasing the clod.” In the corpus it belongs to a recurrent animal comparison: “the lion bites the person; the hound chases the clod.” The phrase appears as an appraisal after exchanges and in admonitions such as “you must be a lion that bites the person; do not imitate the hound chasing the clod.” Related forms call people “mad dogs chasing the clod” and say “chasing the clod and tracking the scent does not yet make a good dog.” The headword occurs 326 times across 148 allowlisted texts.
Senses.Note: The hound and mad-dog variants share one literal image and one corpus deployment; they are not separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 直須師子咬人，莫學韓獹逐塊
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An admonition states the corpus's own contrast: be the lion that bites the person, not the hound chasing the clod.
Case verse preserves the compact lion/hound antithesis.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「獅子咬人，韓盧逐塊。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master gives the paired phrase as his appraisal of a monk's move in public exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如此等輩，皆是狂狗逐塊，何曾夢見有獅子奮迅的牙爪
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address expands the image into mad dogs chasing a clod and contrasts them with a lion's teeth and claws.
A rebuke pairs chasing the clod with tracking scent and denies that this makes a good dog.
